Course 15

Motivation and habits

What drives us, how habits form, how to set useful goals and what to do about procrastination.

Lesson 4. Procrastination and willpower

1 · Lesson

To procrastinate is to voluntarily delay something we intend to do, despite knowing it harms us. It is not usually laziness or poor time management, but a way of avoiding unpleasant emotions linked to the task: boredom, insecurity, fear of doing it badly.

The idea that willpower is a "tank" that runs down with use was very popular, but large attempts to replicate it have produced weak or null results. What does seem clear is that people with more self-control do not resist more temptations; they face fewer, arranging their surroundings so they do not have to struggle.

Useful strategies: start with a very small step (two minutes), remove friction from what we want to do and add it to what we want to avoid, be kind to yourself after a delay (harsh self-criticism increases procrastination) and break big tasks into dated parts.

2 · Example

A study with university students found that those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before a first exam procrastinated less when preparing for the next one. Blaming yourself does not motivate as much as it seems; forgiving yourself makes it easier to return to the task.

3 · Activity

Choose a task you have been putting off for days. Write down what emotion thinking about it causes. Then define the smallest possible first step and do it today for just two minutes.

4 · Check
5 · Going further
